items.content:
RT @AdamCohen8: Story time about how ‘Extreme Ownership’ by @jockowillink and @LeifBabin changed me. 

I was in basic cadet training (BCT) at the US Air Force Academy as a 17-year-old. 

About two weeks in, one of our flight cadre (cadet version of military training instructor) started yelling at me to cup my hands. I was pretty sure I was cupping my hands correctly so I didn’t know what to do. 

I came into basic having marched competitively at a very high level through Civil Air Patrol and jROTC. This made me confident that I wasn’t doing anything wrong. 

Finally I just opened my hands and put them back the way I was doing it before. He replied “thank you” so that seemed to confirm that he just wanted to yell at me for something. 

Then I got covid (this was in 2020) and was isolated from my flight for a week. While in isolation, they allowed us to sit in the bleachers to watch our flights march in a ceremony. 

During the ceremony I got to see the cadre that was correcting me march for the first time. Before this, I was always in the formation and couldn’t see him. 

His marching was objectively terrible. He was swinging his arms way too far forward and not bringing them back past the front of his thigh. 

This confirmed to me that he had no idea what he was talking about and must have been yelling at me for the sake of yelling. 

I returned to my flight after a week and continued the cycle of getting yelled at to cup my hands and repeating my solution from earlier. 

One day, I guess he caught on that I wasn’t changing anything and he erupted at me. As he was berating me, he accidentally spit on my face and I recoiled. This pissed him off further and he sent me up the chain for what the military calls a “verbal counseling.”

In the verbal counseling, I met a MSgt that I am eternally grateful to. He let me tell the story you just read without interrupting. 

Then he replied, “why did you never tell him that you didn’t understand his critiques?” 

I said that I thought he was just looking for something to yell at me for. Other than this I was performing very well. I realized as I was saying it, that if that was the case, it wouldn’t have escalated to this. 

I realized that even though I was objectively correct in terms of the marching and he was mistaken in his corrections, I could have handled the situation better. 

The MSgt asked me if I had ever read Extreme Ownership. I said that I had heard of it but never read it. He spent some time summarizing the lessons of the book and I wanted to know more. 

Basic during Covid meant we had to sit through a lot of briefings on Teams via our laptops from our dorm rooms. 

While I was supposed to be listening to briefings, I found a way to read the book on my computer. That night, the cadre forgot to take our laptops away from us and I stayed up till 2 AM to finish the book. 

It completely changed the way I view leadership. Now, whenever something goes wrong, I do my best to only think about what I could have done differently to cause a different outcome. 

I worked basic as flight cadre going into my junior and senior years. Both times, I kept a copy of the book on me and read several passages to my flight. 

This experience also made me a better cadre. Most people think that the job is just about yelling at people and being scary. It’s not. It’s about training them to transition from being a civilian to a member of the military. 

I kept my intensity at a 10 the whole time and never let an infraction slide, but I never made up a reason to yell. 

If you yell all the time, your yelling becomes meaningless. But if you reserve yelling for when it is absolutely necessary to convey the seriousness of the matter, it carries so much more weight. 

Anyways, thanks for listening to my TED talk. Happy Thanksgiving!

Researchers: Yihao Yang, Pengfei Qiu, Chunlu Wang, Yu Jin, Dongsheng Wang, and Gang Qu, explored hidden Performance Monitoring Unit(PMU) events in Intel CPUs. These are undocumented performance counter events that exist in the hardware but Intel didn't document. 

They found a large number of hidden PMU events that can be associated with microarchitectural behaviors. The events are exploitable as side channels for transient execution attacks. They recovered private data using hidden PMU side channels that weren't supposed to exist in the official documentation. Whether these hidden PMU events correspond to unknown hardware components in the microarchitecture remains unanswered. Intel documented some events officially but left hundreds of others completely hidden.

items.content:
RT @zoecyber001: 19 years of BitLocker lockout just collapsed to 20 days because of a $1 motherboard flash chip.

Firmware TPMs on modern laptops store failed PIN counts on external SPI flash. TPM 2.0 Dictionary Attack Protection enforces a 32-try limit followed by one guess every 10 minutes, relying on a JEDEC counter called RPMC inside that flash chip to stop state rollbacks.

 At ACM CCS 2026, researchers broke that lock on both sides.
On Winbond RPMC flash (25R and 74M chips), a 1-second voltage glitch leaks the HMAC signing key straight out of the chip. Any laptop using that flash, Intel or AMD, now accepts forged counter values and rolls back its failed-attempt state.

On AMD fTPM (CVE-2026-43613), the firmware skips verifying whether the counter ever incremented. A custom interposer sitting between the CPU and SPI flash blocks counter updates with zero glitching.

 Measured worst-case brute-force results on locked laptops:
  * 4-digit Windows Hello PIN: 69 days down to 40 hours
  * 6-digit BitLocker startup PIN: 19 years down to 20 days

Winbond has no patch timeline because fixing the leak takes new silicon. AMD published AMD-SB-7079 with firmware fixes rolling out from November 2026 through February 2027.

items.content:
Small followup, what I didn't mention in the original post is that I looked for my own sandbox escape, and .. found it. I reported it that same day to Docker and on Nov 10 they said they would allocate CVE-2026-126139 (which never happened). But I see it was fixed partially in v0.53.0 and fully in v0.54.0 ¯\_(ツ)_/¯

Imagine you deploy a sandbox with a runtime mount sourced from a subdirectory of its workspace. Code in the sandbox could then replace the parent of the mount source with a symlink. Initially, the mount remained attached to the original directory, but after an automatic idle period or later restore, it would retarget through the symlink, allowing read/write access to an arbitrary host path outside the sandbox workspace. The redirect also survived sandbox restarts. If many sandboxes used the same workspace (which is likely), any instance could retarget the mounts of all other instances, making this a cross-sandbox attack as well.

In v0.53.0, Docker partially mitigated the broader issue by validating static mount sources and inconsistent saved metadata. However, this did not close the runtime-mount problem.

In v0.54.0, Docker added the missing check. If a saved mount source resolves to a different directory, SBX refuses to start the sandbox.

RT @superalesha: I deleted Linux completely, baked Qwen3-0.6B into a 24 KB pure x86-64 assembly OS, and it runs up to 54% faster than native Linux llama.cpp.

The entire Multiboot OS binary (asm-llm-os.elf) is 24,252 bytes, written from scratch without Linux, Windows, C, Rust, or libc. It boots in 74 to 94 ms straight into 64-bit Long Mode, wakes every CPU core over APIC, maps the 614 MiB Q8_0 weights directly from physical RAM, and drops you into a live multi-turn KV-cache chat over VGA, PS/2 keyboard, and serial.

I ran head-to-head CPU benchmarks against llama.cpp (Q8_0, -ngl 0) on the same AMD EPYC 7642:

- 1 thread hits 23.67 tok/s vs 16.63 (+42%)
- 4 threads hit 78.89 tok/s vs 51.08 (+54%)
- 8 threads hit 118.08 tok/s vs 80.79 (+46%)
- 16 threads hit 134.94 tok/s vs 103.03 (+31%, 136.6 peak)

On a diskless 0 GB Proxmox VM (2014 12-core Intel Xeon E5-2670 v3, 2 GiB RAM), it boots straight to the prompt in under 5 seconds (95 ms kernel boot) and runs live out of RAM at 78 tok/s decode and up to 111.5 tok/s prefill, with a hybrid BIOS+UEFI ISO builder included too. Output stays bit-exact across thread counts and matches all 64 greedy tokens against PyTorch FP32 (0.99965 cosine).

The 14.7 KB Linux ELF build (FAST_Q8=1 INT8xINT8 AVX2+F16C) also beats llama.cpp by 18% to 36% from 1 to 40 threads, and booting bare metal with 2 MiB huge pages squeezes out another 10% on top.

RT @BitcoinNewsCom: RUMORS OF AI BREAKING MODERN CRYPTOGRAPHY INTENSIFY

Computer scientist Scott Aaronson says he has heard multiple rumors that OpenAI or Anthropic, or both, have discovered a polynomial-time algorithm for integer factorization.

Ledger’s CTO has now confirmed hearing similar rumors surrounding three major cryptographic breakthroughs at frontier AI labs:

• INTEGER FACTORIZATION IN P: A sufficiently efficient algorithm would break RSA encryption without requiring a quantum computer, threatening banking systems, government communications, digital authentication, software signing and much of the world’s digital infrastructure.

• ELLIPTIC CURVE CRYPTOGRAPHY (ECC): Bitcoin does not rely on RSA but instead relies on elliptic curve cryptography for its digital signatures. A practical breakthrough here could allow attackers to derive Bitcoin private keys from exposed public keys and steal funds using ordinary computers. Bitcoin’s SHA-256 hashing and proof-of-work mining would not necessarily be compromised.

• RING-LWE: A breakthrough undermining its quantum resistance could compromise a major mathematical foundation of post-quantum cryptography, jeopardizing parts of the world’s ongoing migration to quantum-resistant systems.

Unlike quantum computing, an efficient classical attack on RSA or ECC could potentially be distributed as software and executed on conventional computers worldwide.

Perhaps the bigger concern is what such discoveries would reveal about AI’s ability to solve foundational mathematical problems that have resisted decades of human research.

Ledger’s CTO remains skeptical that any of these cryptographic primitives have been completely broken but acknowledges that responsibly disclosing such a discovery without triggering mass exploitation would be extremely difficult.

All three rumors remain unverified.
